# How to Add Numbered Captions and Cross-References in Google Docs

> **In short:** Google Docs now has three tools for figures, tables, and equations: inline captions that number themselves, cross-references that update when a caption changes, and a clickable table of captions. Google says the tools also work with Word (.docx) files.

Picture finishing a long report, then realizing you added a chart on page 3. Now every "Figure 4" after it is wrong, and you have to fix each one by hand. Google's new features are built to stop that kind of cleanup.

## Before you start

You need a Google account and a document you can edit. Google says the features are available to Google Workspace customers, Workspace Individual subscribers, and people with personal Google accounts. If you use Workspace through a work or school account, you don't need to ask your admin for anything, because Google says there is no admin control for this feature. It is on by default.

A few terms first:

- **Caption**: the short label under a figure or table, such as "Figure 1: Monthly sales."
- **Inline caption**: a caption that carries a number Google Docs manages for you.
- **Cross-reference**: a link in your text that points to a caption, like "as shown in Figure 2."
- **.docx**: the standard Microsoft Word file format. Google says you can view and edit these files directly in Docs.

## Step 1: Open your document and pick a figure or table

Open a document that already has an image or table in it. Click the spot where you want the caption to go. Tip: place the caption where the reader will expect it, usually right below the image or table.

Next, go to **Insert**, then **Page elements**, then **Inline caption**. Google's help menu lists the path this way, so look for those three names.

**You'll know it worked when** a numbered label, such as "Figure 1," appears in the spot you chose. You can type your own description after it.

## Step 2: Write a caption that makes sense on its own

Once the label is in place, type a short description after it. Keep it to one line when you can, so readers can scan the page quickly.

💬 Example caption text: "Figure 1: Monthly sales by region, January to June"

Good captions say what the reader is looking at, not how it was made. "Sales chart" is fine. "The chart I made on Tuesday" is not.

**You'll know it worked when** the label and your description appear together and the number is already filled in for you.

## Step 3: Add a second caption and watch the numbers update

Scroll to another figure or table, click where its caption belongs, and go to **Insert**, then **Page elements**, then **Inline caption** again. Google says these labels order and renumber themselves as captions are added, moved, or removed.

To test it, add a new caption above the first one. The first label should change from "Figure 1" to "Figure 2," and the one that was "Figure 2" should move to "Figure 3."

💬 Try this: add a caption to a new image near the top of your document, then scroll down to see the later numbers shift.

**You'll know it worked when** every caption is numbered in the order it appears on the page, without you typing a single number.

## Step 4: Link to a caption with a cross-reference

Now let's point to a figure from your text. Place your cursor in the sentence where you want the reference, then go to **Insert**, then **Page elements**, then **Cross reference**. Choose the caption you want.

Why not just make a regular link? A standard hyperlink keeps the text you typed, even if the target moves. Google says the display text of a cross-reference updates to match the caption it points to. If Figure 2 becomes Figure 3, your sentence follows along.

💬 Example sentence: "Sales rose most in March, as shown in Figure 2."

**You'll know it worked when** the reference shows the caption's current label, and clicking it moves you to that figure or table.

## Step 5: Add a table of captions

At the start of your document, or in a spot that suits your layout, click where you want the list. Go to **Insert**, then **Page elements**, then **Table of captions**.

Google says this creates a clickable list of your captions with page numbers. The list is organized by label type, so your figures appear together and your tables appear together. Readers can jump straight to any item from this list.

**You'll know it worked when** a list appears with your captions, page numbers, and grouping by label. Clicking an entry should take you to that item.

## Step 6: Edit, then check everything

Make some real changes to test the system. Delete one figure, move another, and rewrite a sentence that includes a cross-reference. Then scroll through the whole document and check three things: the caption numbers, the words in each cross-reference, and the table of captions.

Google says these elements update as you edit, but a quick scan is still worth it before you send the file. If you work on a document with others, do this check after their edits too.

💬 Quick check: search your document for the word "Figure," then make sure each mention matches a real caption.

**You'll know it worked when** every number and reference matches the current layout, and the table of captions lists items in the right order.

## Common mistakes

- **Mistake: typing "Figure 3" by hand.** Typed numbers won't update when you move things around. **Fix:** delete the typed label and use **Insert**, then **Page elements**, then **Inline caption** so Google manages the number.
- **Mistake: adding a cross-reference before you have any captions.** There is nothing to link to yet. **Fix:** insert at least one caption first. Google says the cross-reference and table of captions options need at least one caption in the document.
- **Mistake: using a regular link to point at a figure.** Regular links keep their old text after you move things. **Fix:** use **Insert**, then **Page elements**, then **Cross reference** instead.
- **Mistake: expecting the table of captions to show anything when it's empty.** The list is built from your captions. **Fix:** add captions first, then insert the table and check it again after your last edits.

## What this means for you

- **In everyday life**: If you write a school paper, lab report, or club newsletter with charts and photos, use inline captions so your figure numbers stay correct when you rearrange pages.
- **For your business or work**: If you write contracts, proposals, or technical drawings, these tools help keep references to exhibits and schematics accurate. Google specifically mentions contracts and schematics as documents where manual updates were a problem.
- **If you're just getting started**: Begin with Step 1 on one document. Add a single caption, then a single cross-reference. That's enough to see how it works.
- **If you already use it**: Google says you can use custom labels, not just "Figure" or "Table." For example, you could create an "Exhibit" label for a contract, then use cross-references throughout the text and generate one table of captions near the end.

## Wrap-up

Google Docs now handles the numbering, linking, and listing of your figures, tables, and equations, so you don't have to fix them by hand after every edit. Start with one image: insert an inline caption, add a cross-reference to it in your text, then insert a table of captions and see how the three work together. Open a document you already have and try it today.
